newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan, Iraq agree on extra trade.
newsitem.headline: Jordan, Iraq agree on extra trade.

text.p: Jordan and Iraq have agreed to increase trade over the winter to meet sanction-hit Baghdad's urgent food requirements and cover extra heating needs in fuel-hungry Jordan, businessmen and officials said on Monday.
The official Petra news agency said Jordan pledged late on Sunday to supply Iraq with $35 million worth of goods in addition to the $200 million agreed in a 1996 trade protocol.

It said the extra supplies, mainly food and detergents exempt from U.N. trade sanctions imposed on Baghdad for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, would count as an advance against next year's trade protocol, whose value has yet to be fixed.

"To ensure the continuity in flow of basic Jordanian commodities to the Iraqi market for the rest of the year the two sides agreed to allocate the sum of $35 million to import vegetable oils, detergents, soap and fertiliser to be covered by the 1997 protocol," Petra said.
The deal was reached at a meeting between Jordan's Minister of Trade and Industry Ali Abu al-Ragheb and visiting Iraqi Trade Minister Mohammed Mehdi Saleh, it added.

Trade Ministry officials declined to give details, but Jordanian businessmen say Iraq, hit by delays to a $2 billion oil-for-food deal, has been seeking an increase of around $50 million in next year's protocol with Jordan.
The oil-for-food deal was agreed on in May but was held up by Washington after a showdown over Baghdad's intervention in Kurdish faction fighting in the north of the country.
Under Jordan's 1996 accord with Iraq, over $200 million was deposited in an escrow account at Jordan's Central Bank to pay Jordanian firms for exports of food and medicine to Iraq.
In return, Jordan received around 70,000 barrels of low-priced Iraqi oil per day.

Khaldoun Abu Hassan, chairman of the Amman Chamber of Industry who returned from a trip to Baghdad last week, said Iraq had also pledged to raise supplies of gas and some oil products to Jordan over the winter months.

"They promised to double the average quantity of gas in winter," Abu Hassan said, without giving details of the quantities involved. "There are other products which they have the capacity to export to us like aviation fuel and base oil for our lubricant plant," he told Reuters.
Abu Hassan said Iraq was also able for the first time since 1990 to supply Jordan with fuel for gas lighters.
Jordan slashed the volume of protocol trade with Iraq this year from around $400 million in 1995 after King Hussein turned against President Saddam Hussein, calling for change in Baghdad.
Officials say that Jordan is unwilling to increase the protocol agreement next year because the system of payment for Jordanian firms drains valuable foreign currency reserves from the Central Bank.
But Abu Hassan said increasing trade with Iraq would give a major boost to the Jordanian economy.
"This year I hope we will provide more (to Iraq) because that would help the industry and transportation sectors," he said. "That also (helps) banking and commercial sectors."
He said Iraqi officials had "emphatically reconfirmed" that if trade restrictions with Iraq start to be lifted, Baghdad would encourage imports through Jordan's Red Sea Aqaba port.
"Aqaba will be treated on an equal footing with (Iraq's Gulf port at) Umm Qasr," he said.
